newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales jump, reopening inflation debate.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales jump, reopening inflation debate.

text.p: The British government said on Wednesday that retail sales surged higher last month but insisted inflation remained firmly under control.
The Office for National Statistics said sales rose 0.6 percent in January for a year-on-year increase of 4.6 percent.
The annual figure was the highest since March 1989 -- sales of clothes and furniture were particularly strong -- and well above market expectations.
"The underlying economy is picking up momentum. It's going to continue to fuel arguments from the Bank of England for a rate hike at some stage," said David Brown of Bear Stearns.

Analysts had expected a 0.3 percent monthly rise and a year-on-year increase of 3.9 percent. The surprise jump in high-street sales, following a disappointing run-up to Christmas, pushed stock prices and the British pound higher.
Analysts predicted fresh pressure for an interest rate hike but the Treasury said the data did not signal a new inflationary threat in what has been a steady and strong economic comeback.

"The in-control recovery continues. High street sales remain on a healthy upward path, with January sales providing an all-round welcome winter warmer for the British economy," said Economic Secretary to the Treasury Angela Knight.

The government says there is no need for a rate hike yet and is eager to fight the election, which must be held by May 22, on a ticket of strong growth coupled with steady rates. Experts say its economic record is its best bet for re-election as it trails the opposition Labour Party by some 20 points.

Knight -- whose department has repeatedly clashed with the central bank over the threat posed by rising prices -- insisted in an interview with Reuters there were few signs of inflationary pressures in the pipeline.

"Of course we look at the improvement in sales, the improvement in manufacturing," she told Reuters Financial Television. "We take into account some of the other factors, like for example, there is very little sign of any sort of inflationary pressures in the pipeline for raw materials and so on, and there is the strength of the pound."
The Bank of England might see things differently.

At their regular meeting last month, central bank governor Eddie George strongly advised Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates by a quarter point, according to minutes of the talks released on Wednesday.

"The Bank still thought it was likely that a monetary tightening of a half of a percent would be needed fairly soon to moderate the growth of domestic demand," the minutes show him as saying. "But the Bank did strongly recommend a quarter percent rise this month," the minutes said.
Clarke, however, held out, pointing to the strong pound.
"The Chancellor said he did not believe that enough account had been taken of the strength of the exchange rate."
